Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. In the WHO European Region, it causes 37% of deaths among women and 31% of deaths among men. Despite this, CVD is still widely perceived as a “men’s disease,” leaving women underdiagnosed, undertreated, and understudied. 🌍 As the World Health Summit explores the future of global health, one thing is clear: equity in cardiovascular care cannot be ignored. At #DaiichiSankyoEurope , our aspiration is that scientific innovation fully values women as patients, healthcare providers, and essential research participants, advancing cardiovascular medicine to really care for every heart. - **A few days ago, I found an old photograph I had not seen in years. It made me smile. It was taken during the communist years in Romania, when many high school students were sent to compulsory agricultural work every autumn. It was not something you chose. You went because you had to. Except that, on that particular day, I did not. Instead of following the others to the fields, I climbed onto a district heating pipe and walked away. Someone happened to catch the moment on camera. I am sure I did not think of it as a big statement at the time. I was probably just trying to avoid another long day of work. But looking at the photo now, I recognise something familiar in it: that small, stubborn impulse to move when staying put no longer feels right. Years later, I was sitting in an auditorium with hundreds of young doctors, all waiting to choose where we would spend the next five years of residency. I was supposed to choose neurology in Târgu Mureș, where I had studied, where my friends were, and where life already had a shape. Then my name was called. During that short walk to the microphone, I changed the decision I had been carrying for months. Instead of Târgu Mureș, I chose the very last residency position available in Bucharest. I did not know anyone there. I had no real plan. I just knew I wanted to go. My father asked the most reasonable question: "How do you think you're going to live in Bucharest on a resident's salary?" And he was not wrong. At the time, a resident earned roughly one hundred US dollars a month. It was just enough to rent a tiny one-room apartment, with almost nothing left for food, transport, or much else. The first months were hard. Money was short, the city felt big, and I knew almost nobody. More than once, I wondered whether I had made a terrible mistake. In the end, Bucharest changed my life in ways I could not have imagined then. A few weeks ago, that old feeling came back. After more than twenty years in Pricing and Market Access, I realised I missed learning in a way that made me a little uncomfortable. I missed asking new questions, having different conversations, and not always being the person who already knows what to do. It would have been easier to stay. I enjoyed the work, learned from wonderful colleagues, and will always be grateful for everything those years gave me. I could not explain it perfectly, at least not in a way that would fit neatly into a pros and cons list. But I knew the feeling. So I chose to listen to it. Maybe that is what the photograph reminded me of. Some decisions only start making sense later, after you have already begun walking.**
